question: What are design principles and why do they matter from the start?
title: Design Principles Fundamentals
direct_answer: Design principles such as SOLID, DRY, KISS, and YAGNI are guidelines for placing responsibilities, dependencies, duplication, and complexity. They help developers discuss why code is hard to change and choose safer boundaries. They are context-dependent heuristics, not laws or proof that a design is good.

sections.title: Principles are design checks, not rigid laws
sections.content:
Design principles give a team a shared vocabulary for common change problems. **SRP** asks where a responsibility belongs. **OCP** looks for a stable extension point. **LSP** protects subtype contracts. **ISP** keeps client dependencies focused. **DIP** separates policy from implementation details.

**DRY** targets duplicated knowledge, while **KISS** and **YAGNI** resist unnecessary complexity and speculative features. These ideas can pull in different directions. Removing duplication can create a premature abstraction; adding an interface for every class can make a small program harder to follow.

Use principles as questions during a concrete change: which rule is duplicated, which client depends on this method, which variation is real, and which behavior does the contract promise? Tests, change history, domain knowledge, and operational needs provide the evidence. A pattern name alone does not make a design correct.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content: The core ideas: (1) SOLID — SRP (a class has one reason to change), OCP (open for extension, closed for modification), LSP (subtypes substitutable for base types), ISP (no forced unused dependencies), DIP (depend on abstractions); (2) DRY — 'don't repeat yourself'; every piece of knowledge has a single representation, or duplication breeds maintenance bugs; (3) KISS — keep it simple; the simplest correct solution wins; (4) YAGNI — 'you aren't gonna need it'; don't build for hypothetical requirements; (5) each principle prevents a specific rot — SRP prevents god-classes, OCP prevents edit-everywhere, DRY prevents duplicate maintenance, KISS/YAGNI prevent over-engineering; (6) they are heuristics, sometimes in tension (DRY vs. KISS can conflict), resolved by context.

sections.title: Design Principles and What Each Prevents
rows: Split a class doing too much
Editing many files for one change

sections.title: SOLID applied to one small class
Trade-offs & When It Matters
sections.content: The central tension is that principles sometimes conflict: DRY (eliminate duplication) can conflict with KISS (a little duplication is simpler than a wrong abstraction) — the resolution is to extract when the duplication is of knowledge (the same rule in three places), not of coincidence. A second tension: SOLID pushes toward abstraction (interfaces, injection), which adds indirection that KISS/YAGNI warn against — apply SOLID when there's a real variation, not preemptively. The third: principles are heuristics, not laws; rigidly applying all of them to a one-off script over-engineers it. They guide, and context decides which dominates.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Design principles (SOLID, DRY, KISS, YAGNI) are checks against code rot — readable, changeable, correct as code grows.
SRP: a class has one reason to change; prevents god-classes that change for unrelated causes.
OCP + DIP: extend via abstractions so new behavior needs no edit to existing code.
DRY: every piece of knowledge has one representation; duplication breeds maintenance bugs.
KISS/YAGNI: the simplest correct solution wins; don't build for hypothetical requirements.
content: Design principles help reason about change, responsibilities, dependencies, and complexity.
SOLID addresses module and contract design; DRY addresses duplicated knowledge.
KISS and YAGNI challenge unnecessary or speculative machinery.
Principles can conflict, so context and evidence decide the trade-off.
Use them as review questions, not rigid rules or a checklist of patterns.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Design principles are guidelines that help a team make code easier to understand and change. SOLID covers responsibilities, extension points, subtype contracts, focused interfaces, and dependency direction. DRY addresses duplicated knowledge, while KISS and YAGNI challenge unnecessary complexity and speculative functionality.

For example, repeated payment branches may suggest Strategy and OCP, but an interface for a behavior with one stable implementation may add no value. Likewise, extracting two similar lines may satisfy a shallow view of DRY while coupling two business rules that need to evolve separately.

The principles are not laws and do not replace tests or domain understanding. I apply them to a concrete change: identify what varies, who owns the rule, which contract clients rely on, and whether an abstraction reduces the real cost of change. The best design is the simplest one that preserves the required behavior and leaves known changes manageable.

question: What is the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)?
title: Single Responsibility Principle Explained
direct_answer: The Single Responsibility Principle says a class or module should be responsible to one main actor or cohesive concern, giving it one primary reason to change. It can have many methods, but they should change together for the same purpose. Mixing HTTP handling, business rules, persistence, and email delivery usually creates several independent reasons to change.

sections.title: Understanding Single Responsibility Principle
sections.content:
The **Single Responsibility Principle** says a software module should have one primary reason to change. A practical interpretation is that it should serve one actor or cohesive concern. The principle is about change boundaries, not one method per class.

A Spring controller can translate HTTP input and output, an application service can coordinate a use case, a repository can handle persistence, and a mail adapter can talk to an email provider. If an email-template change and a database change both require editing the same class, unrelated policies have become tangled.

Layers are only a starting point. A service can still contain several unrelated business policies, and an overly fragmented design can create needless navigation. Keep behavior together when it changes together; separate it when different owners, policies, or technologies cause independent change.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|One Reason to Change|~SRP core rule|class owns a single concern|change in one concern → one class edited|the 'S' in SOLID
blue|Violation Smell|~god class|HTTP + DB + email in one class|name has 'And' or 'Manager'|unrelated imports mixed
emerald|The Fix|~split by concern|Controller / Service / Repository|each class one axis of change
violet|Payoff|~maintainability|smaller blast radius|easier to test and read

sections.title: SRP Violation vs Compliant Design
When to Apply SRP
sections.content:
Apply SRP when designing any new class — ask yourself: **what is this class's single job?** Use it when you catch yourself writing a class that needs imports from multiple unrelated packages like javax.mail, java.sql, and org.springframework.web in the same file.

Apply SRP during code reviews when you see method names that hint at multiple concerns: saveAndEmail(), validateAndStore(), or parseAndNotify(). It's especially critical in **service layers** where it's tempting to mix business logic, persistence calls, external API calls, and notification logic. In Spring Boot apps, SRP naturally emerges when you use **@Service** for orchestration, **@Repository** for data access, and separate utility classes for formatting or validation. If a class is hard to name without using 'And' or 'Manager', it likely violates SRP and needs splitting.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing SRP with 'one method per class'**: Freshers often think SRP means tiny classes with single methods, leading to absurd over-granularity. A UserRepository with save, findById, delete is perfectly SRP-compliant because all methods serve one responsibility: User data access.
- **Naming classes with vague suffixes**: Using names like UserManager, DataHandler, or ServiceHelper hides the real responsibility. These become dumping grounds for unrelated methods.
- **Mixing layers in one class**: Putting @RestController, business logic, and @Repository annotations on the same class violates SRP by mixing presentation, domain, and persistence concerns. Each layer is a separate reason to change.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: SRP gives a class or module one primary reason to change.
The responsibility is a cohesive concern or actor, not a single method.
Keep behavior together when it changes for the same reason.
Separate HTTP, business policy, persistence, and external-service concerns when they change independently.
Avoid both God Classes and one-method-class fragmentation.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The Single Responsibility Principle says a class or module should have one primary reason to change. In practical terms, its methods should serve one cohesive concern or actor. It may have several methods; they belong together when the same policy change affects them.

For example, a controller can translate an HTTP request, an order service can apply the order use case, a repository can persist orders, and a notification adapter can call an email provider. If endpoint formatting, tax rules, SQL mapping, and email templates all live in one class, independent changes collide and tests need unrelated setup.

SRP is not a command to create one class per method. The useful boundary follows change: keep code together when it evolves together, and separate concerns that have different rules, owners, or external dependencies.

question: How do you identify an SRP violation in existing code?
title: Identifying SRP Violations in Java Code
direct_answer: Identify an SRP violation by listing the independent reasons, actors, or policies that can change a class. Mixed responsibilities often show up as unrelated dependency groups, methods that use disjoint fields, or tests that require unrelated setup. File length, import count, field count, and names containing 'and' are clues only—not numeric rules or proof.

sections.title: Detecting SRP Violations in Real Code
sections.content:
Start with **change reasons**, not size. Ask who requests changes to this class and which policy each change belongs to. A class edited for API shape, pricing rules, database mapping, and notification templates has several independent pressures.

Then inspect the structure. Methods may form separate clusters that use different fields; dependencies may belong to unrelated systems; tests for one rule may require setting up another concern. These are stronger clues than a line count because a long parser can still have one focused purpose, while a short utility can mix unrelated jobs.

Names such as `saveAndEmail` or a mixture of web, persistence, and messaging code can start the investigation, but none proves a violation. Trace actual change history and business ownership before splitting. Extract a class when the new boundary has a clear responsibility and useful contract.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Ask why|~List change reasons|which actor asks?|which policy changes?|do changes happen independently?
blue|Look for clusters|~Methods + fields|separate dependency groups|unrelated test setup|mixed external systems
emerald|Check evidence|~History and ownership|files changed together|bugs cross concerns|review boundaries
violet|Refactor carefully|~Extract one concern|name its contract|move tests with it|avoid arbitrary tiny classes

sections.title: Identifying SRP Violations Through Code Smells
When to Apply Detection Techniques
sections.content:
Review SRP when unrelated feature changes repeatedly touch the same class, merge conflicts collect there, or a test for one policy requires configuring unrelated systems. Examine change history and dependency clusters before splitting.

Do not split by an arbitrary line, field, or mock count. A useful extraction owns a recognizable concern and can be named without vague words such as `Helper` or `Manager`. After the change, the classes should have clearer reasons to change rather than merely being smaller.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using file size as proof**: a long cohesive parser may be fine, while a short class can mix policies.
- **Treating imports or field count as numeric rules**: look for independent dependency clusters and change reasons.
- **Splitting on vague names alone**: confirm the boundary with usage and change history.
- **Producing smaller classes with no clear responsibility**: extraction should make ownership and contracts clearer.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: List the independent actors, policies, or technologies that can change the class.
Look for method and field clusters that barely interact with each other.
Unrelated dependencies and test setup are useful warning signs.
Line count, import count, and field count are clues, not thresholds.
Use change history and ownership to choose a meaningful extraction.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I identify an SRP violation by asking which independent reasons can change the class. If endpoint representation, pricing policy, SQL mapping, and email templates all require edits to one class, it is serving several concerns.

The code often confirms that result: one group of methods uses a repository, another uses a mail client, and another only formats HTTP responses. Tests for pricing may need unrelated mail or database setup. Those clusters suggest boundaries such as a pricing policy, repository adapter, and notification service.

Size and counts are not rules. A large parser can be cohesive, and a small utility can mix unrelated behavior. I use change history, ownership, dependencies, and method-field relationships as evidence, then extract only when the new class has a clear responsibility and contract.

question: How does SRP improve testability of Java classes?
title: SRP and Unit Testability in Java
direct_answer: SRP can improve testing by isolating one policy from unrelated infrastructure and reducing irrelevant setup. A pricing rule can be tested with a small input instead of booting web, database, and mail components. This is a common benefit, not a guarantee: focused classes can still need collaborators, and integration tests remain necessary for wiring and real boundaries.

sections.title: How SRP Enables Easier Testing
sections.content:
When a class owns one cohesive concern, its tests can focus on that concern's inputs, outputs, state changes, and collaborations. Splitting a pure pricing policy from persistence and email often lets the policy run as a plain unit test with no Spring context.

This improves failure diagnosis: a pricing assertion points to pricing logic, while repository and mail adapters have their own contract or integration tests. It can also reduce mocks, but mock count is not a formal SRP measure. Orchestrators legitimately coordinate several ports, and some responsibilities are integration boundaries by nature.

`@SpringBootTest` is not evidence of bad design. It is appropriate for verifying application wiring and cross-component behavior. The warning sign is needing the entire application only to test a small business rule that could have a clearer boundary.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Fewer Dependencies|~SRP effect|one concern → few collaborators|fewer mocks to set up
blue|Pure Logic|~zero mocks|validator = input/output asserts|no DB or email stubbing
emerald|Isolated Failures|~clear signal|broken test → known responsibility
violet|Smell|~test pain|setup longer than the test → split it

sections.title: Testing SRP-Compliant vs Violating Classes
When Testability Drives SRP Application
sections.content:
Use the test suite as design feedback when a small rule cannot be exercised without unrelated web, database, or messaging setup, or when failures in one concern make unrelated tests fail. Extracting a policy or adapter can create a clearer test boundary.

Keep integration tests for application wiring and external boundaries. Do not split classes only to reach a chosen mock count or test length; check whether the extracted responsibility has a coherent purpose.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating fewer mocks as the definition of SRP**: test setup is evidence, not a rule.
- **Replacing every collaborator with a mock**: simple values or fakes may express a contract more clearly.
- **Calling every Spring integration test a design failure**: use integration tests for wiring and real boundaries.
- **Splitting without a cohesive responsibility**: smaller classes are useful only when their purpose is clearer.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Focused classes reduce unrelated setup in tests.
Pure policies can often run as fast unit tests without Spring or infrastructure.
Separate adapter tests can cover database, HTTP, and messaging boundaries.
Mock count and test length are signals, not SRP rules.
Integration tests remain necessary for wiring and real component interaction.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
SRP often improves testability because a test can exercise one concern without constructing unrelated parts of the application. If `TaxPolicy.calculate(order)` is a focused rule, a JUnit test can pass an `Order` and assert the amount without starting Spring, a database, or a mail server.

Persistence and notification adapters can then have their own integration or contract tests, while a use-case service tests the coordination between its required ports. Failures are easier to locate because each test has a narrower reason to fail.

This is not a numeric rule about mocks or setup lines. A focused orchestrator may legitimately have several collaborators, and `@SpringBootTest` is valuable for verifying real wiring. The design smell is unrelated setup needed to test one small policy, not the mere presence of integration tests.

question: What is the difference between SRP and separation of concerns?
title: SRP vs Separation of Concerns in Java
direct_answer: Separation of Concerns is the broad idea of organizing a system so distinct concerns are handled in distinct parts, from modules and layers down to functions. SRP is a more specific change-oriented principle: a class or module should be responsible to one main actor or cohesive concern. They support each other but are not simply architecture versus classes.

sections.title: Distinguishing SRP from Separation of Concerns
sections.content:
**Separation of Concerns (SoC)** is the broad practice of keeping distinct concerns in distinct places. A system might separate user interface, application rules, persistence, and infrastructure into modules or layers. The idea can also apply inside a class or function.

**SRP** focuses the boundary through change responsibility: a class or module should be responsible to one main actor or cohesive concern and therefore have one primary reason to change. SRP is commonly discussed for classes, but it is not limited to them.

The ideas overlap without being identical. A layered application may have good SoC at the package level while one service still mixes pricing, notification, and auditing. Conversely, splitting code into many folders does not create either property if changes still cut across every part. Evaluate actual responsibility and coupling, not labels.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Separation of concerns|~Broad organizing idea|distinct policies and technologies|works at many scales|reduces entanglement
blue|Single responsibility|~Change-oriented test|one main actor or concern|class or module|one primary reason to change
emerald|Possible mismatch|~Labels are not proof|good layers + God Service|small classes + tangled modules|inspect real changes
violet|Use together|~Choose boundaries|separate distinct concerns|keep cohesive work together|verify dependency direction

rows: Mixing presentation and DB in same layer
One class handling HTTP and SQL

sections.title: When to Apply Each Principle
sections.content:
Use **Separation of Concerns** when making architectural decisions: should we split into microservices? How do we organize packages? Should frontend and backend be separate repos? Apply SoC when defining **module boundaries**, deciding what goes in the service layer vs the controller layer, or structuring packages like com.app.domain, com.app.infrastructure, com.app.api.

Use **SRP** when writing or reviewing individual classes: does this UserService class belong in the business layer or is it mixing data access? Should validation logic live in the controller or a separate validator class? Apply SRP during **refactoring** when you find classes that are hard to name or test. In Spring Boot projects, SoC guides your use of annotations like @RestController, @Service, @Repository to enforce layer separation. SRP guides what methods go in each of those annotated classes. Both principles work together: SoC creates the container structure, SRP fills it with well-designed classes.

Use SoC for the 30,000-foot view, SRP for the 10-foot view.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Reducing the distinction to architecture versus classes**: both ideas can apply at several scales.
- **Trusting layer names**: a service package can still contain mixed policies.
- **Equating more folders with better separation**: boundaries should reduce real coupling and change collisions.
- **Fragmenting cohesive behavior**: keep code together when it changes for the same reason.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: SoC broadly separates distinct concerns across a system at many scales.
SRP focuses on one main actor or cohesive reason to change for a class or module.
SRP is not limited to classes, and SoC is not limited to architecture.
Layer names do not prove the responsibilities are separated.
Use both ideas to keep unrelated changes from colliding.

sections.title: Code Example
Interview answer
sections.content:
Separation of Concerns is the broad principle of placing different concerns in distinct parts of a system. It explains boundaries such as presentation, application rules, persistence, and infrastructure, and it can be applied at architecture, module, class, or function level.

SRP is more specific about change responsibility. A class or module should serve one main actor or cohesive concern, giving it one primary reason to change. A service that mixes pricing policy and email-template rendering can violate SRP even when it sits inside a correctly named service layer.

SoC helps identify categories of work; SRP tests whether one unit owns too many independently changing categories. They reinforce each other, but folders and layers alone are not proof—the real evidence is which rules, owners, and dependencies change together.

question: Can a class have multiple methods and still follow SRP?
title: Multiple Methods and SRP Compliance in Java
direct_answer: Yes — a class can have many methods and still follow SRP as long as all those methods serve the same single responsibility. A UserRepository with save, findById, delete, and update has four methods but one responsibility: data access for User. Method count is irrelevant; concern count is what matters.

sections.title: SRP and Method Count Are Independent
sections.content:
The **Single Responsibility Principle** is about **concern count, not method count**. A class can have ten, twenty, or fifty methods and still perfectly comply with SRP — as long as all those methods relate to the same single responsibility.

Consider a **CustomerRepository** with methods like save, findById, findByEmail, findByLastName, update, delete, existsById, and count. That's eight methods, but they all serve one cohesive responsibility: **data access for Customer entities**. The class has one reason to change: when the way we store or retrieve Customer data changes. Contrast this with a three-method class that validates input, sends an email, and logs to a database — despite having only three methods, it violates SRP because those three concerns are unrelated and would change for independent reasons. The word 'single' in Single Responsibility refers to having **one axis of change**, not a limit on functionality. Think of **cohesion**: all methods in an SRP-compliant class collaborate toward the same goal. A naive interpretation that restricts classes to one method would force you to create hundreds of tiny classes with names like UserSaver, UserFinder, UserDeleter — making navigation and understanding the codebase nightmarish. SRP is about **semantic unity**, not artificial size constraints.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Concern Count|~what matters|not method count|all methods → one responsibility
blue|Compliant|~cohesive class|Repository: save/find/update/delete|one concern: data access
emerald|Violation|~few methods, many concerns|validate + email + log = 3 reasons
violet|Naming Test|~remove half the methods|name still fits → cohesive

sections.title: Multi-Method Classes Following SRP
When Multi-Method Classes Are Appropriate
sections.content:
Multi-method classes are appropriate when all methods serve a **cohesive responsibility** — repositories, validators, formatters, calculators, and adapters naturally have many methods.

Use them in **repository patterns** where CRUD operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete) plus query variations all relate to data access for one entity.

Apply in **service orchestration** where multiple public methods represent different workflows but all coordinate the same domain concern. In **utility classes**, many static helper methods for one data type (StringUtils with trim, capitalize, truncate, format) are fine. Multi-method classes shine in **Spring Data JPA** repositories where you define findByX, findByY, existsByZ — all querying the same entity type. The key test: **if you removed half the methods, would the class name still make sense?** If your UserValidator lost validateEmail but kept validatePassword and validateAge, it's still a validator. That's cohesion.

Avoid multi-method classes when methods operate on **different data types** (one method takes Orders, another Customers) or have **unrelated side effects** (some methods query databases, others send HTTP requests, others write files).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing method count with responsibility count**: Freshers often think SRP means one method per class, leading to absurd over-granularity like UserSaver, UserFinder, UserDeleter classes instead of one cohesive UserRepository with all related methods.
- **Accepting utility dump classes**: Allowing classes like Utils, Helper, or Manager to grow to hundreds of methods serving unrelated purposes just because 'SRP allows multiple methods.' Those violate SRP because the methods don't share a single responsibility.
- **Forcing artificial splits**: Breaking a cohesive 15-method repository into five separate classes just to reduce method count, which increases complexity without any design benefit and makes the codebase harder to navigate.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **Cohesion over count**: Ten methods serving one responsibility is better than three methods serving three unrelated concerns
**Responsibility definition**: SRP's 'single' refers to one reason to change, not a limit on functionality or method count
**Repository example**: A repository with save, findById, update, delete, exists, count is perfectly SRP-compliant
**Semantic unity test**: All methods should collaborate toward the same cohesive goal, like data access or validation
**Naming test**: If you removed half the methods, would the class name still describe what remains? If yes, it's cohesive

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Yes, absolutely. A class can have many methods and still follow SRP. The principle is about having one responsibility, not one method. Method count is irrelevant. What matters is whether all those methods serve the same cohesive concern. A good example is a repository. A UserRepository might have save, findById, findByEmail, update, delete, exists, and count. That's seven methods, but they all do the same thing: manage data access for User entities. The class has one reason to change — if the database schema changes or we switch databases, all those methods might need updating, but they change together because they're part of the same responsibility. Contrast that with a class that has just three methods, but one validates input, another sends emails, and the third writes to a log file. That's three unrelated concerns, so even with fewer methods, it violates SRP. The key is cohesion. All the methods in an SRP-compliant class should be working toward the same goal. One pitfall is thinking SRP means you need tiny classes with one method each. That would give you UserSaver, UserFinder, UserUpdater classes, which is absurdly granular and makes the codebase a nightmare to navigate. Focus on one responsibility, not one method. If every method in your class relates to the same concern, you're good, no matter how many there are.
